reasons: UNSUPPORTED: "Before he turned ten, Huang was scrubbing toilets at a Kentucky reform school (Oneida) that his uncle had mistaken for a prestigious boarding school" (Britannica says he was nine when he and his brother were sent to their uncle in Tacoma. It says the uncle 'shortly thereafter' sent them to Oneida, and that his parents collected them about two years later. The uncle's mistake and the daily toilet cleaning are confirmed. Nothing says he was still nine, or under ten, at Oneida. Fix: drop 'before he turned ten' or say 'at nine or ten'. Britannica gives no age for Oneida itself.)

UNSUPPORTED: "Fox Business reported the milestone on 30 October" (The article metadata says created 2025-10-30. The visible page says 'Published October 31, 2025'. The page was also modified on 4 Nov. Imprecise. Either drop the date or say 'on 29 October NVIDIA closed at a $5.03 trillion value, Fox reported'.)

UNCITED: "'That figure is the company's market valuation, not a measure of Huang's own wealth, and this page does not give a net-worth estimate.' This is an editorial caveat. It is fine, but it has no tag."

Reviewer recommends rejection: Nearly every claim checks out against the cited sources. Two things need fixing before approval. (1) The opening claim that Huang was cleaning toilets at Oneida 'before he turned ten' is not supported. Britannica says only that he was nine when sent to Tacoma and went to Oneida 'shortly thereafter'. It gives no age at Oneida. Reword to match the source, for example 'at nine or ten'. (2) 'Fox Business, reporting the milestone on 30 October' does not match the page, which shows 'Published October 31, 2025'. The milestone itself was on Wednesday 29 October. Use the correct date or drop it. Minor: replace the editorialising 'Huang is blunt about how much he expects from AI' with something neutral, and make clear the tattoo was not in 1999.

claims.claim: Before he turned ten, Huang was scrubbing toilets at a Kentucky reform school (Oneida) that his uncle had mistaken for a prestigious boarding school
claims.note: Britannica says he was nine when he and his brother were sent to their uncle in Tacoma. It says the uncle 'shortly thereafter' sent them to Oneida, and that his parents collected them about two years later. The uncle's mistake and the daily toilet cleaning are confirmed. Nothing says he was still nine, or under ten, at Oneida. Fix: drop 'before he turned ten' or say 'at nine or ten'. Britannica gives no age for Oneida itself.

claims.claim: He and his brother had been sent over from Thailand alone; Oneida took in children labelled 'difficult'
claims.note: Britannica says they were sent to live with their uncle in Tacoma while their parents stayed in Thailand. It calls Oneida a reform school for 'difficult' children. 'Alone' is a fair inference. It is not stated outright.

claims.claim: Born Jen-Hsun Huang on 17 February 1963 in Tainan, Taiwan, second son of a chemical engineer and a grade-school teacher (also facts.birthDate and facts.birthPlace)
claims.note: Britannica gives the date, the place, the second-son detail and the parents' jobs. CHM confirms 1963 and Tainan.

claims.claim: Family moved to Thailand when he was five; parents did not plan to stay because of the Vietnam War; father had been accepted into a Carrier worker-training programme; mother taught 10 English words a day
claims.note: All details match Britannica.

claims.claim: At nine he and his brother were sent to an uncle in Tacoma, then to Oneida; he cleaned toilets daily, his brother worked on a tobacco farm, and the other students bullied them
claims.note: Matches Britannica.

claims.claim: About two years later the parents arrived, found out what the school was and took the boys out; the family settled near Portland, Oregon; at Aloha High School he played competitive table tennis, earned a national ranking and graduated in 1981
claims.note: Matches Britannica.

claims.claim: Bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Oregon State University, 1984; met fellow engineering student Lori Mills there, and the two later married
claims.note: Matches Britannica. NVIDIA's bio also confirms the OSU BSEE.

claims.claim: Worked at AMD for about a year, then LSI Logic from 1985 to 1993, eventually becoming director of a division; later earned a master's in electrical engineering at Stanford while working
claims.note: NVIDIA's bio gives LSI Logic 1985-1993 and AMD 1984-1985. Britannica gives the director role and the Stanford master's earned while working.

claims.claim: NVIDIA was founded on 5 April 1993 by Huang, Malachowsky and Priem to bring 3D graphics to gaming and multimedia
claims.note: NVIDIA's timeline gives the exact date, the three founders and the stated aim.

claims.claim: Malachowsky and Priem, fellow chip designers, picked Huang as CEO; they started with $40,000 and soon raised an initial $20 million from venture capital firms, which carried the company through a hard first few years
claims.note: Matches Britannica. The article attributes the 'carried the company through' judgement to Britannica.

claims.claim: Huang has been president, CEO and a board member since the start
claims.note: NVIDIA's bio page, fetched 2026-10-26, still lists him as co-founder, president and CEO, so the claim is current.

claims.claim: NVIDIA went public in 1999; Huang had the logo tattooed on his left shoulder when the stock hit $100; he has said he probably would not get another
claims.note: Matches Britannica. Minor risk: placing the tattoo right after the 1999 IPO sentence could imply it happened in 1999. Britannica gives no date for the tattoo.

claims.claim: The same year (1999) the company launched the GeForce 256, which CHM calls the world's first GPU, combining transform, lighting and rendering; NVIDIA's history dates the invention of the GPU to 1999 (also the summary)
claims.note: Both sources match.

claims.claim: Through the early 2000s steady performance gains made NVIDIA the leading supplier of graphics chips for gamers and professionals
claims.note: Matches CHM.

claims.claim: CUDA released in 2006 as a platform for general computing on NVIDIA GPUs; universities and national laboratories soon used the chips in some of the world's fastest supercomputers
claims.note: Matches CHM.

claims.claim: In 2012 NVIDIA GPUs powered AlexNet, which the company points to as the start of modern AI, and NVIDIA turned to accelerated computing for AI (also the summary)
claims.note: CHM gives the 2012 AlexNet use and the pivot. NVIDIA's timeline gives the 'era of modern AI' wording.

claims.claim: Chips built for game graphics turned out to be well suited to running machine-learning algorithms
claims.note: Matches Britannica.

claims.claim: CHM's profile says most AI models today, from large language models to driving systems, are trained and run on NVIDIA technology
claims.note: Matches CHM. The CHM page was last modified in May 2024, so 'today' reflects 2024. It is attributed to the museum, which is acceptable.

claims.claim: In 2018 NVIDIA introduced RTX, which it describes as the first GPU capable of real-time ray tracing
claims.note: Matches NVIDIA's timeline, and the article attributes the description to the company.

claims.claim: CHM quotes Huang calling AI the technology industry's 'single greatest contribution to social elevation'
claims.note: The quote is on the CHM page. The lead-in 'Huang is blunt about how much he expects from AI' is the article's own characterisation (see style note).

claims.claim: At the 2018 GTC in San Jose Huang said GPUs were 25 times faster than five years earlier, outpacing Moore's law; the press named it 'Huang's law'
claims.note: Matches Britannica.

claims.claim: Fortune named Huang Businessperson of the Year for 2017; Harvard Business Review put him first on its 2019 list of the world's 100 best-performing CEOs over the lifetime of their tenure
claims.note: NVIDIA's bio says the same. Britannica words the HBR item more loosely (world's best-performing CEO in 2019). The article uses the more precise NVIDIA wording.

claims.claim: Time included him among the 100 most influential people of 2021
claims.note: Matches Britannica.

claims.claim: CHM made him a 2024 Fellow for leadership in devices and systems for computer graphics, accelerated computing and AI
claims.note: CHM page title and citation confirm the 2024 Fellow award and the wording.

claims.claim: Huang and his wife founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation in 2007; per Britannica it has given to their alma maters, public health initiatives and San Francisco Bay Area organisations (also the FAQ on his wife)
claims.note: Matches Britannica. It says the foundation 'made donations'. The article's 'has given' is acceptable. The FAQ says they met as engineering students at OSU, which is also in Britannica.

claims.claim: In late October 2025 NVIDIA became the first company to reach a $5 trillion market valuation; shares had risen about twelvefold since ChatGPT launched in 2022
claims.note: Fox says the milestone came on Wednesday (29 Oct 2025) and gives the twelvefold rise since ChatGPT's 2022 launch, citing Reuters. A past event, so not outdated.

claims.claim: Fox Business reported the milestone on 30 October
claims.note: The article metadata says created 2025-10-30. The visible page says 'Published October 31, 2025'. The page was also modified on 4 Nov. Imprecise. Either drop the date or say 'on 29 October NVIDIA closed at a $5.03 trillion value, Fox reported'.

claims.claim: On 11 December 2025 Time named the 'Architects of AI' its Person of the Year; eight people, six first-time recipients, including Huang, Sam Altman and AMD's Lisa Su
claims.note: The AP piece is dated 11 Dec 2025 and says there are eight people with six first-time recipients, naming Huang, Altman and Su. 'Six weeks later' after 30 Oct is accurate.

claims.claim: Huang himself had spent a year at AMD after graduating in 1984
claims.note: Britannica says about a year. NVIDIA's bio gives 1984 to 1985.

claims.claim: In 2026 IEEE gave him its Medal of Honor 'for leadership in the development of graphics processing units and their application to scientific computing and artificial intelligence'
claims.note: Quote and year match the IEEE recipient page (19 words).

claims.claim: IEEE describes the medal as its most prestigious award; Huang was presented with it at the IEEE Honors Ceremony in New York City
claims.note: IEEE says presented in April 2026 at the Honors Ceremony in New York City. It calls the medal its most prestigious or highest award. The IEEE Spectrum source (listed in person.json, not cited in the body) agrees.

claims.claim: FAQ: Born 17 February 1963, which makes him 63 as of 26 October 2026
claims.note: Arithmetic is correct: 63 after 17 Feb 2026. The Britannica page itself is stale (it shows age 61), but the birth date is the same.

claims.claim: FAQ: Huang, Malachowsky and Priem founded NVIDIA in April 1993 and chose Huang as CEO; he studied at Oregon State (BS EE 1984) and Stanford (MS EE); Tainan birth, Thailand at five, US at nine
claims.note: The same facts are confirmed above. The FAQ gives no tags, but the body supports each answer.

claims.claim: Summary and knownFor: Taiwan-born American engineer, co-founder, president and CEO of NVIDIA
claims.note: NVIDIA's bio supports the roles. Britannica says 'entrepreneur'. 'Engineer' is backed by his EE degrees.

valueNote: It has a clear biographical timeline from Taiwan and Thailand to Kentucky, Oregon and NVIDIA, built mostly from primary or authoritative sources (NVIDIA, CHM, IEEE, AP). It puts the 2025 and 2026 honours in context and connects the AMD detail across sections. It avoids hype and does not put a net-worth number on a high-risk topic. The voice is concrete and varied, with no em dashes or banned hype words. One small voice problem: 'Huang is blunt about how much he expects from AI' is the article's own characterisation, not a sourced opinion.
